## Introduction {.unnumbered}

The ability to work confidently with data is increasingly important in almost every profession. Organisations use data to understand what has happened, identify patterns, compare groups, evaluate decisions and make predictions about the future. However, working with data involves more than calculating statistics. It also requires you to ask sensible questions, select appropriate methods, interpret results carefully and communicate your findings clearly to others.

This group presentation gives you an opportunity to bring together the skills developed throughout this course. Your group will investigate a dataset, address a research question and communicate the results through a short presentation. You should use a combination of numerical summaries, tables, visualisations and inferential statistical methods to develop a clear and evidence-based answer.

### Forming a group and selecting a topic {.unnumbered}

First, form a group of **four or five students**. Once your group has been formed, select one of the 21 topics listed below. Each topic is accompanied by a dataset containing one main outcome variable and a range of possible explanatory variables.

Once you have decided who is in your group, fill out this form:

[Group Project Form](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/19hkKKvoNZ7KjxoOL8yVr6g6qFEe3a23i-gDnttqcRpo/edit?gid=0#gid=0)

You do not need to examine every variable in the dataset. Instead, identify the variables that are most relevant to your research question and use these to develop a focused analysis.

topics |>
  mutate(
    Download = map_chr(file, \(f) as.character(
      download_file(
        path = file.path("data", f),
        output_name = tools::file_path_sans_ext(f),
        button_label = "Download",
        button_type = "success",

### Preparing an effective presentation {.unnumbered}

A strong presentation is selective. Avoid filling slides with every calculation or output that your group produced. Instead, include the evidence that is most useful for answering the research question.

When preparing your slides:

-   use graphs and tables that can be understood quickly;
-   explain results in the context of the scenario rather than only reporting numbers;
-   distinguish between statistical significance and practical importance;
-   avoid claiming that an association proves causation;
-   ensure that your conclusions match the statistical evidence; and
-   rehearse as a group so that the presentation is coherent and remains within the time limit.

The aim is not simply to demonstrate that your group can calculate statistics. The aim is to show that you can use statistics to investigate a meaningful question and communicate what you have learned.
